newsitem.title: USA: Florida cabinet backs Keys sanctuary plan.
newsitem.headline: Florida cabinet backs Keys sanctuary plan.

text.p: Florida's cabinet Tuesday approved a plan to create an environmental preserve in the Florida Keys despite emotional appeals from residents who said they feared a federal "takeover" of the island chain.

By a unanimous vote, the cabinet approved plans to establish the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary, a 2,800-square-mile refuge off Florida's southern coast. Its approval was critical to the success of the federal sanctuary because about 65 percent of its area lies in state waters.

The Keys coral reef, one of the world's largest reef tracts, lures about 1.5 million visitors a year. Once a pristine marine habitat, it has been badly damaged in the last two decades by pollution, overdevelopment of the Keys and careless divers and fishers.

Many Keys residents oppose the sanctuary, saying it would be the first step toward a federal takeover. Thousands of residents make their living from tourism and fear restrictions on fishing rights and land use.

Keys residents are known for their fierce independence. In the early 1980s, the Keys staged a mock secession from the United States in response to federal roadblocks designed to catch drug smugglers at the entrance to the island chain.

Deterioration of the reef has been a growing concern for federal lawmakers, who approved the sanctuary after a series of ship groundings in 1989 caused extensive damage and highlighting the ecosystem's fragility.

Bettye Chaplin, vice president of the Conch Coalition set up to oppose the plan, said residents feared the loss of local control over the Keys. A non-binding referendum on the issue in November found 55 percent of Keys voters opposed the plan.
"We had the largest voter turnout we've had in 15 years. ... If our vote in America doesn't count, what counts?" Chaplin asked at the cabinet meeting.
But after the cabinet's unanimous vote, supporters wearing "Sanctuary Yes" sashes applauded and hugged one another. Many were crying.
"It's been a six-year struggle. The Keys is a complex ecosystem with a lot of problems," said Dave Holtz, director of the Centre for Marine Conservation's Keys office.
The cabinet vote cleared the way for final federal approval and a Florida Marine Fisheries Commission review of zoning regulations needed to set up the sanctuary.
